title: The best laws the many could bear
source_text: Ἐὰν δέ τις ἐν τούτοις δεισιδαιμονίαν μᾶλλον ἢ πονηρίαν περὶ τοὺς πολλοὺς τῶν πιστευόντων τῷ λόγῳ εἶναι φαντάζηται καὶ ἐγκαλῇ ὡς δεισιδαίμονας ποιοῦντι τῷ λόγῳ ἡμῶν, φήσομεν πρὸς αὐτὸν ὅτι, ὥσπερ ἔλεγέ τις τῶν νομοθετῶν πρὸς τὸν ἐρωτῶντα, εἰ τοὺς καλλίστους ἔθετο τοῖς πολίταις νόμους, ὅτι οὐ τοὺς καθάπαξ καλλίστους ἀλλ᾿ ὧν ἐδύναντο τοὺς καλλίστους· οὕτω λέγοιτο ἂν καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ πατρὸς τοῦ Χριστιανῶν λόγου ὅτι ὧν ἐδύναντο οἱ πολλοὶ εἰς βελτίωσιν ἠθῶν τοὺς καλλίστους ἐθέμην νόμους καὶ διδασκαλίαν, πόνους οὐ ψευδεῖς ἀπειλῶν καὶ κολάσεις τοῖς ἁμαρτάνουσιν ἀλλ᾿ ἀληθεῖς μὲν καὶ ἀναγκαίους εἰς ἐπανόρθωσιν τῶν ἀντιτεινόντων προσαγομένους, οὐ μὴν καὶ πάντως νοούντων τὸ τοῦ κολάζοντος βούλημα καὶ τὸ τῶν πόνων ἔργον· καὶ τοῦτο γὰρ πρὸς τὸ χρήσιμον καὶ κατὰ τὸ ἀληθὲς καὶ μετ᾿ ἐπικρύψεως συμφερόντως λέγεται. πλὴν ὡς ἐπίπαν οὐ πονηροὺς ὑπάγονται οἱ τὰ χριστιανισμοῦ πρεσβεύοντες. ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ ἐπηρεάζομεν εἰς τὸ θεῖον· λέγομεν γὰρ περὶ αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀληθῆ καὶ τοῖς πολλοῖς σαφῆ μὲν εἶναι δοκοῦντα οὐ σαφῆ δ᾿ ὄντα ἐκείνοις ὡς τοῖς ὀλίγοις, φιλοσοφεῖν ἀσκοῦσι τὰ κατὰ τὸν λόγον.
pass_a_gloss: But if anyone imagines (φαντάζομαι) that in these there is superstition (δεισιδαιμονία) rather than wickedness (πονηρία) among the many of those believing (πιστεύω) the word, and accuses our word as making people superstitious (δεισιδαίμονες), we shall say to him that, just as one of the lawgivers (νομοθέται) said to the one asking whether he had laid down (τίθημι) the finest (κάλλιστοι) laws for the citizens, that not the finest absolutely (καθάπαξ) but the finest of those they could [receive]; so it might be said also by the father [= author] (πατήρ) of the Christians' word: of those the many could [receive] for improvement (βελτίωσις) of characters (ἤθη) I laid down the finest laws and teaching (διδασκαλία), threatening (ἀπειλέω) to sinners (ἁμαρτάνοντες) pains (πόνοι) and punishments (κολάσεις) not false (ψευδεῖς) but true and necessary (ἀναγκαῖοι), applied (προσάγω) for the correction (ἐπανόρθωσις) of those resisting (ἀντιτείνω), though they do not altogether understand (νοέω) the intention (βούλημα) of the one punishing and the work (ἔργον) of the pains; for this too is said for usefulness (πρὸς τὸ χρήσιμον) and according to truth and with concealment (μετ᾿ ἐπικρύψεως) profitably (συμφερόντως). However on the whole those championing (πρεσβεύω) the things of Christianity do not lead on the wicked. Nor do we insult (ἐπηρεάζω) the divine (τὸ θεῖον); for we say about it things true, and to the many seeming clear (σαφῆ), yet not being clear to them as to the few, who practise (ἀσκέω) philosophising (φιλοσοφέω) the things according to the word.
pass_b_english: But suppose someone imagines that, in these matters, it is superstition rather than wickedness that marks most of those who believe the word, and he charges our word with making people superstitious. We shall say to him that one of the lawgivers, when asked whether he had laid down the best laws for his citizens, replied, “Not the best absolutely, but the best of those they could receive” (Plutarch, Life of Solon 15). So too the father of the Christian doctrine might say: “I have laid down the best laws and teaching that the many could receive for the improvement of their character. I threaten sinners with pains and punishments that are not false, but true and necessary, and brought to bear for the correction of those who resist, even though they do not wholly understand the purpose of the one who punishes, or what the pains are meant to do.” For this too is spoken for their benefit, both in keeping with the truth and, to good purpose, with something held back.

Yet, on the whole, those who uphold the teachings of Christianity do not lead on the wicked. Nor do we insult the divine. For what we say about it is true; and to the many it seems clear, though it is not as clear to them as it is to the few who give themselves to studying the things of the word with philosophy.

choices.choice: Copy-text: staged source_3.json section 79 (Koetschau 3.79). The lawgiver's answer is the saying Plutarch gives to Solon (Life of Solon 15.2: the best laws the Athenians would accept); Origen names only 'one of the lawgivers', so the name stays in the citation, not the text. 'ὧν ἐδύναντο' (of those they could) has no infinitive; 'receive' supplied by sense, as the Greek requires one. 'ὁ πατὴρ τοῦ Χριστιανῶν λόγου' is the Platonic idiom 'father of a discourse' (its author); reviewer set it lowercase, as in 3.75, so the English does not decide between God (giver of the laws and threats, the likelier reading) and Christ (author of the teaching). The speech is Origen's hypothetical, given in quotation marks as direct speech; it is not Celsus. 'μετ᾿ ἐπικρύψεως' (with concealment/reserve) rendered 'with something held back'. 'τὸ θεῖον' kept as 'the divine', answering Celsus's charge of insulting God. No Scripture quotation or clear allusion.

'the Father of the Christian doctrine' set lowercase as 'the father of the Christian doctrine' (Platonic idiom for the author of a discourse; the capital decided a referent the Greek leaves open), matching 3.75
Restored 'προσαγομένους', dropped in the draft: punishments 'true and necessary, and brought to bear for the correction of those who resist'
Classical citation written in full as '(Plutarch, Life of Solon 15)'
Checked: the hypothetical speech is Origen's, not Celsus's; 'νοούντων' correctly tied to those who resist; negation 'not false but true' exact
